video_title: Are Rates and Breadth Warning About a Bankpocalypse Crash
gist: Weekly Jordi Visser speed-round arguing that rising rates with weak breadth is not a dot-com repeat because mega-cap tech (56% of market cap) is rate-insensitive, breadth is a washout/bottoming signal, and AI disruption drives a coming bank apocalypse as consumer agents and crypto rails take hold.

themes.theme: Rates up, breadth down is not 2000

insights.claim: Visser argues rising rates with weakening breadth is rational today and not a repeat of the dot-com bubble: the 2009-2022 period of negative-yielding bonds should be excluded from yield comparisons, and the current move looks scary only against that distorted baseline.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bond-yield bear cases built on pre-2022 history are comparing to an abnormal regime.
insights.quote: it is insane to me that people are sitting there saying that this is going to be like the.com bubble

insights.claim: Nominal GDP is about 6.5%, which he calls below the midpoint of a normal range for the 10-year; he would only start worrying about bonds as a long-term problem if yields rise decisively above 7%, though higher yields hurt some parts of the market.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete trigger level (~7%) for when rates become a genuine problem.

insights.claim: Tech and AI-related mega caps (Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta, Tesla and similar) are now 56% of market cap versus just over 10% at the financial crisis, and 78 companies make up 56% of the market; these firms are non-cyclical and not hurt by rates moving from 5% to 5.3%, which is the main reason rates matter less than before.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Index-level rate sensitivity has fallen because the index is dominated by rate-insensitive digital businesses.

insights.claim: The old economy is rate-sensitive but tiny and slow: GM plus the four major homebuilders had revenue of $333B in 2015 and $432B now (about 2.4% CAGR), while Nvidia plus Micron went from $21B to $535B in revenue combined. Visser says those old-economy names deserve to fall when rates rise and need rates to go down.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive sectors are a small and stagnant share of earnings, so their weakness drags breadth without hitting the economy.

insights.claim: Nvidia's expected revenue increase next year (roughly $300B, from about $410B to about $700B by his rounding) is about equal to the entire annual revenue of the GM-plus-homebuilder group, which he cites as proof of how different the economy is from pre-2015.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Single-company incremental revenue now dwarfs whole legacy sectors.

insights.claim: Financial conditions historically tightened when rates rose from 1971 to 1999, but since then the relationship has disappeared; the 2022 rate shock did not cause a recession and the Silicon Valley Bank episode did not change the economics, so a rolling one-year rise in yields and Fed funds should not be read as a recession signal.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Don't use tightening-of-financial-conditions models calibrated on old data.

insights.claim: Breadth weakened because the yield curve move was a bear flattener, with short rates rising fastest on Fed-hike expectations. That shifted when John Williams signaled no October hike and PCE and payrolls came in weaker, so he expects breadth to stabilize and improve after earnings season as companies report no dramatic damage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fed-hike repricing was the proximate driver of the breadth selloff, and its reversal is a catalyst.

themes.theme: Breadth as a contrarian bottoming signal

insights.claim: Staples versus the S&P is making new lows now, unlike the 2008-2023 pattern in which breadth selloffs coincided with staples rallying. Visser attributes the old pattern to negative-yielding bonds pushing investors into staples and utilities, and says real defensive rotation would be the warning sign to watch for.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A rotation into defensives, not weak breadth alone, would signal real risk-off.

insights.claim: Staples and utilities are the sectors showing spikes in new 52-week lows, while tech shows no spike in new lows; he reads this, citing The Compound and Friends and chartkidmatt, as typical of a market bottom, and notes equal-weight tech made an all-time high on the day.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Washout is concentrated in non-growth sectors, which is constructive for the AI trade.

insights.claim: The 14-day RSI of market breadth hit the 25 level; he back-tested instances since 2004 when it hit or broke below 25 and says forward returns, particularly six-month returns outside the financial crisis, are heavily skewed to the upside, so he sees breadth as a bottoming sign rather than a negative.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Oversold breadth historically precedes positive six-month returns.

insights.claim: The latest breadth readings: 20-day measure up to 74 (highest since the peak), 50-day at 69, a decisive turn above the 200-day moving average, and the average distance from 52-week highs still about 20%, which he expects to keep falling.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Internal market health is turning up after the washout.

insights.claim: Strategists who called for a broadening-out trade this year are wrong and he suggests they hope for a crash to be bailed out; trades like long Europe/short US unwound as rates and oil rose and weak sectors underperformed, while the AI trade kept defying doubters.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Consensus broadening and anti-US positioning has been the wrong side of this tape.

insights.claim: Equal-weight versus cap-weight S&P correlates with ISM; the bounce happened, but oil rose first and then rates rose, which hit the equal-weight trade. Had rates stayed low he thinks the broadening trade would have continued through year-end, but he says those names do not matter to the economy.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Oil and rates, not AI fears, explain the broadening trade's failure.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 has a breakout chart and NDX made new all-time highs; NDX over S&P is rising, and the S&P has consolidated since June when the AI trade broke down. He expects a break higher after consolidation, and says macro participants lose money because anti-crypto/anti-AI trades (long gold, copper, commodities, the dollar) show no trend.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fading crypto and AI in favor of gold or commodities has been costly.

themes.theme: Disruption winners and losers in equities

insights.claim: Visser believes all equities are vulnerable over the next five years, but first small businesses that don't supply AI infrastructure must be eliminated and replaced by AI-native businesses; he says every trade is a disruption trade and the alpha is in shorting the vulnerable 440 names rather than assuming their decline takes down the whole economy.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Breadth weakness reflects disruption, so short the disrupted rather than fear a systemic crash.
insights.quote: The alpha is on shorting the 440

insights.claim: Breadth is poor because earnings are missing for homebuilders, autos and staples, which he sees as disrupted by AI; he adds that Ford and GM should have been gone long ago but were propped up, and that tokenization will take the market from the Mag 7 to a 'mag billion' of growth companies.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Expect legacy industrials and consumer names to keep underperforming structurally.

insights.claim: Visser says a bank apocalypse is starting, comparing it to the software apocalypse of Q3/Q4 last year: banks (BKX closed below its 200-day) will see multiple compression rather than going out of business, and he views a Q1 story. Software names that bounced remain in a perma bear market on valuation.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Banks likely rerate lower as agents and crypto rails erode fee pools.
insights.quote: there's a bank apocalypse that is starting just like I talked about a SAS apocalypse

insights.claim: He sees zero chance that Visa and Mastercard are long-run beneficiaries of agentic payments, though they may benefit for the next two years; he compares them to BlackBerry versus the iPhone, arguing agents and AI-native businesses will use cheaper, instantly settling crypto rails and the trust argument for incumbents will fail.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Short or avoid payment incumbents on a multi-year view despite near-term resilience.

insights.claim: Visser says AI inference/token demand keeps growing and the 'AI bubble' call has been wrong for two years; his 10-name concentrated portfolio is up 106% for the year. He cites a16z's State of the Markets and notes every Nvidia chip is supposed to depreciate like a car yet demand continues, so every GPU-obsolescence headline has been a poor reason to sell.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bubble framing has cost investors; own the tech earnings, not the bubble narrative.

insights.claim: Micron's revenue jumped about elevenfold per his slide, and management said it sees no line of sight to supply catching up with demand because larger models, longer context, concurrency and agents drive memory needs. Visser says he started buying Micron back in the 800s and is still in, with a position smaller than Marvell, Nvidia or crypto; he notes he wrote in May 2025 when Micron was $98 and it is now over $1,000.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Memory remains a core scarcity trade in his AI infrastructure basket.

insights.claim: Rogers (chemicals/materials) took its numbers up in a step function at an investor day, from roughly $3 to $14 in the figures he showed; he highlights step-up stories with supply constraints and says power density and heat density now matter as the Rubin era focuses on efficiency and watts.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Thermal and materials suppliers are second-order beneficiaries of the compute build.

insights.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic combined actual revenue this year (about $100B, not ARR) will exceed the entire software sector's revenue, and the increase this year is larger than the rest of software's increase, implying AI is taking budget from other categories.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: AI lab revenue growth is cannibalizing software spend.

themes.theme: Consumer agents, crypto rails and the bank thesis

insights.claim: Visser calls personal/consumer AI agents a new demand inflection as important as enterprise agents in late 2025: the Instinct AI founder said compute demand effectively doubles weekly, they already run about $1B annualized transaction volume (50% travel), users reach 80% retention after connecting sensitive information, and compute is hard to buy with lead times of months.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Agent adoption adds a new layer of token and memory demand beyond coding agents.

insights.claim: Mag 7 firms previously had separate lanes in the attention economy, but in the agent economy they will fight over the same TAM, and Visser expects a feeding frenzy; he notes Google has fallen behind in shipping personal agents, while Meta expanded Muse to small businesses and OpenAI launched a competitor.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Competitive moats from attention verticals weaken in the agent era.

insights.claim: The crypto ecosystem index of 46 tokens has outperformed relative to BKX since Grok-bot and Instinct launched, and crypto has held up while two-year yields rose and Fed hikes were priced; gold broke down. Visser argues this shows crypto is driven by the agent thesis rather than the debasement/liquidity trade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Crypto behaving differently from gold under higher real rates supports a fundamental agent bid.

insights.claim: Joseph Chalum (SharpLink) estimates agents will touch about $4,000 trillion of fees over the next decade for the financial industry (as stated in the transcript), with Ethereum as the settlement layer; Visser cites Larry Fink's 'toll road to tokenization' framing and calls Ethereum effectively the internet, which he says is mispriced.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Ethereum is positioned as agent-finance settlement infrastructure; the fee figure is as stated and unverified.

insights.claim: Speed is a safety feature: settlement delays create risk, as the GameStop episode in January 2021 caused margin-call problems and drove the move to T+1, which took about three and a half years. With agent swarms Visser says money cannot sit in transit, which favors instant crypto settlement over legacy rails.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Faster settlement reduces systemic and counterparty risk, supporting tokenized rails.

insights.claim: Visser says the Peter Lynch approach applies to crypto now: founders like Ilia Pulukin (NEAR, a Transformer co-author) and William Mougayar take calls, big money has not yet invested, and asset manager FOMO is growing; he thinks those who study it over the next two months will have a large advantage over the next year, and he holds an equal-weight 46-token index and personally owns NEAR.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Early-stage crypto-agent infrastructure is where he sees asymmetric opportunity.

insights.claim: Institutional adoption signals this week cited by Visser: Morgan Stanley building a crypto lab, Citi expanding with Coinbase, Franklin Templeton turning tokenized money funds into collateral with Bybit, the SEC five-year transition for tokenized stocks, and Robinhood's AI trading bots. He treats these as evidence of a bank apocalypse underway.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Incumbent banks are scrambling to adopt the rails he says will disrupt them.

insights.claim: He argues equal-weight is wrong for the stock market, where thousands of companies are being disrupted, but right for the 46-token crypto index because money will flow from disrupted banks and software into AI-native businesses that use tokens.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Weighting scheme depends on whether the universe is being disrupted or built out.

insights.claim: Visser reads Bessent as wanting lower rates: Warsh moving higher, the Fed's Williams saying there is no urgency, and Treasury buybacks (he mentions six billion) were warning shots that officials do not want higher rates, though the buyback reaction reversed after day one.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Policy officials are signaling resistance to higher yields, which may cap the rate move.
